# Owner interaction preferences Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase. ## Preferences - **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does. - **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`. - **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc. - **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control. - **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.) - **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of. - **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes. - **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked. # Claudinite — active-pack guidance The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand. # Working discipline The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project. Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution. When the owner asks for a change, don't begin implementing it until the two of you share an explicit understanding of the problem it's meant to solve **and** have agreed that the requested change is the best way to solve it — a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Treat the request as a description of a desired outcome, not a specification to execute on sight; surface your read of the problem, raise a better approach if you see one, and reach consensus first. This applies to any repository, not just this one. An interactive comment from the owner carries one of three build-relevant intents — or none of them — and the classification decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part) — the assessment itself stays judgment. 1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched — the artifact changes as much as the correction demands; what doesn't appear is a new requirement or rule. 2. **A feature** — a feature run: agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes. 3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Once the intent is understood, author the assurance first: the check the future world must satisfy. Execute it and watch it fail — the failure is the evidence it detects exactly what the owner was worried about — and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the same step is demonstrating the gap: show the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it. The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it. A fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for — and an unrouted comment tends to become a one-off patch where a requirement or a rule should have accumulated. Confirm a behavior isn't already provided before building a mechanism for it — verify the gap against a real run first; the cheapest fix is often that it already works. When feedback flags a misunderstanding, don't reflexively expand the artifact to compensate. First check whether it's already correct — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong (the sibling of the rule above). And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs — prose padded to preempt confusion usually breeds it. When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Build from the source, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong; a clean-room rebuild catches biases an edit-in-place pass silently inherits. Fix build/test/CI warnings, don't tolerate them: a clean run with no warnings makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out, so noise here costs detection later. Prefer a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change. Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix: it hides the signal instead of resolving it. Never reach for suppression as the quick path — it's only ever a deliberate, reviewed decision, made once the real fix has been weighed and rejected, never an unattended default. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: an explanation on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected. That inline reason *is* the review record — it's what separates a considered suppression from a reflexive mute, and it's why the suppression needs no second justification recorded elsewhere. Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current. It reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet. When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it (unless one is already open) so it's tracked and not lost — then move on. Resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change. An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; don't carry one approval forward, and don't treat a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt as authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. When in doubt, surface the new state and wait for a fresh approval. # The task lifecycle The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project; this section keeps the method. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill. For every new task: 1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work. 2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`). 3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done. --- # HTML Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model — the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it, and the injected content lands as the `

`'s **next sibling**, leaving the original tag permanently empty. A selector reading `.foo p` silently returns `""` with no error. Read `element.nextElementSibling` instead of assuming the content stayed inside the tag you selected. - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), day-first vs. month-first is genuinely undecidable from the value alone; resolve it once per document, never per source or per field, in this order. (1) **An unambiguous sibling date fixes the page's convention**: a slash date elsewhere on the same page with a part > 12 (e.g. `24/07/2026`) parses only one way, and a page is almost always internally consistent — read that date's order and apply it to every other slash date on the page. (2) Failing that, **read the declared locale** (``, `og:locale`): default **month-first** (the order `Date` and most JS parsers assume, from the US `MM/DD/YYYY` convention) and flip to day-first only on a *positive* non-US signal — a non-US region in `lang` / `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` with unknown region stays month-first rather than guess. The `.` / `-` separators are day-first regardless. - **When code must react to how a real page actually behaves, investigate it live before you ship — don't deploy a hypothesis you can only test after release.** If a change hinges on the real DOM, computed styles, or runtime state of a page you can't see, hand the user one JavaScript snippet to run in the browser DevTools console and read its output back — a single synchronous round-trip that tells you what the page really does. Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for when you've verified the behavior genuinely can't be observed now: a console read costs the user seconds, a deploy-and-check cycle costs a whole release. - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console, say you expect its output, and ask the user to paste it back — that round-trip is the whole ask. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn; the toil you're saving is the user's, so keep it to the code and the paste-back. --- # tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy The nightly PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The fleet routine runs the pack's one maintenance task (`repo-tidy`) against a repo; this is the policy it follows. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md), [single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md), [single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)); the same task also reconciles the standing tracker at the end of its pass. The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.** - **Branches, PRs — assess only.** They may be work in progress. Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete; **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name. - **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive. The `repo-tidy` pass applies each single-object skill across the targets the plan hands it, then rewrites the repo's standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per repo, body rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). --- # EdFringeNow — project working rules Lessons captured while working in this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite canon. Terse and concrete; read the matching one before working in that area. ## Verifying UI changes visually (the `index.html` page and everything under `plan/`) Visual verification of the pages **is** available in this sandbox. Don't skip it or downgrade to "verified by logic review only" claiming no browser exists — a browser is here, and a UI change isn't done until it has been looked at. - Serve the repo and drive it with the preinstalled Chromium (or Playwright): `python3 -m http.server 8000`, then screenshot / click through `http://localhost:8000`. The app fetches `data/shows.json`, so it must be served over HTTP rather than opened as a file — and `localhost` bypasses the agent proxy, so the browser reaches the page even though external hosts need the proxy. - To build a `/plan` favourites list for the render, a plain slug-per-line text file is accepted by the parser — pick shows spanning the statuses (and some same-day doubles) you want to eyeball. - **Never chain `pkill -f "http.server …"` with the rest of a command.** `-f` matches full command lines, so the pattern matches the very shell running the `pkill`: the shell kills itself (exit 144) and everything after the `;` or `&&` — the commit, the verify run, the curl — silently never happens. Every such call in this repo's captured sessions died this way, once misdiagnosed as a heredoc bug. Bracket a character so the pattern can't match its own command line (`pkill -f "[h]ttp.server 8099"`), or just leave the server up and serve the next run on a fresh port. - **Known-noisy console output from the served page.** A page driven off `python3 -m http.server` reliably logs a `favicon.ico` 404 (the repo ships none) and often `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` as the browser tears down. Neither is an application error — filter both out of a smoke script's error assertion so that a red run means something, rather than sending you chasing a phantom 404 through extra browser runs. - To match edfringe.com's live styling (e.g. the ticket-availability colours on the `/plan` grid), fetch the official site's CSS with `curl` through the agent proxy and read the palette out of it. `WebFetch` returns rendered text without the CSS, and headless Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy to reach an external host — `curl` is the one path that works for off-box assets. ## The site is two independent front-ends — cross-page behaviour lives twice The Now page (`index.html` + `js/app.js`) and the planner (`plan/` + `plan/plan.js`) share no code: no modules, no globals, and `plan/lib/` is the planner's own engine, not a common library. So anything that must behave the same on both pages exists as **two copies**, and changing one is only half the change — the UK-bounding-box location guard and the debug menu it gates, the header `debug v` pill, and the Now/Plan nav each live in both files today. Grep the other file for the twin before calling a cross-page change done; it will not fail a test or a parse check. --- # EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/) The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in [scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in [scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working judgment those two don't carry. ## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it `edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and `edfringe.com` returns 403 to `WebFetch`. So: no session — this one included — can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API runs on a GitHub-hosted runner: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow (`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets` scheduled tasks, or the throwaway probe procedure in the `probe-edfringe-api` skill. Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably returns — either run it on a runner, or say plainly that it is unverified. `python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs offline (it is a step in `scripts/verify.sh`); it exercises raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a normalizer change is verifiable here even though a fetch change is not. ## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean "Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the `soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available (`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is carried through for display only. ## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it `data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`, `data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing `scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next `refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator. ## Changing the wire format is a four-file change The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists **by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`, `p[].t`). That encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together: - producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` / `minify_master`) - decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files - decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs` Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand. ## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".

1	// The one vendored place that maps a task's declared model FAMILY to the model
2	// the executor dispatches its subagent at (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §1, §3).
3	// A model-generation bump is a single edit HERE — task files and the executor
4	// only ever speak in families, never concrete ids.
5	//
6	// The resolved value is what the executor passes as the subagent's model. Short
7	// family names are themselves valid model selectors, so they are the safe
8	// default; to pin a task tier to a concrete dated snapshot, change only that
9	// family's value in MODEL_MAP below (nothing else needs to move).
10	
11	export const MODEL_FAMILIES = ['opus', 'sonnet', 'haiku', 'none'];
12	
13	// family → the model the executor dispatches at. `none` is agentless (the worker
14	// is code the scheduler runs inline — no subagent, no model), so it maps to null.
15	export const MODEL_MAP = {
16	  opus: 'opus',
17	  sonnet: 'sonnet',
18	  haiku: 'haiku',
19	  none: null,
20	};
21	
22	// `none` means "pure code, no agent" (DESIGN §1) — the scheduler runs the
23	// worker .mjs inline rather than filing a dispatch issue.
24	export const isAgentless = (family) => family === 'none';
25	
26	// Resolve a family to its concrete model, or throw on an unknown family (the
27	// task-declaration-shape check is the author-time guard; this is the runtime
28	// backstop for the executor/validator).
29	export function resolveModel(family) {
30	  if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(MODEL_MAP, family)) {
31	    throw new Error(`unknown model family "${family}" — valid families: ${MODEL_FAMILIES.join(', ')}`);
32	  }
33	  return MODEL_MAP[family];
34	}

1	# Conversation extract — the growth pack's conversation-side daily task
2	
3	The conversation-side sibling of [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md): mine this repo's captured
4	conversation logs for durable lessons, post a short summary of the exchange behind each extracted rule on the
5	issue it was worked under, and prune logs past retention. You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue. The
6	access model matches growth-extract — the repo's own content is plain **local git** in the checkout; only the
7	GitHub **issue/PR API** goes through MCP. (Capture, which needs the live session transcript, is the separate
8	in-session step at merge; this task consumes what capture already pushed.)
9	
10	The **method** — the friction signals, the measured efficiency analysis, the lesson bar — stays canonical in
11	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) and is not restated here. The captured log carries what
12	that method needs: per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the tool_use/tool_result pairs behind
13	wall-time numbers.
14	
15	## Conventions used in this doc
16	
17	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for the repo's default branch — substitute whatever it uses.
18	- **Access split — local git for repo content, MCP for PRs and the issue API.** Reading the
19	  `conversation-logs` branch and its files, staging the `.claudinite/local/packs/` lesson onto a branch, and
20	  the retention prune are all **plain git in this repo's checkout** (`git fetch`/`show`/`rm`/`push`) — the
21	  branch is *in this repo*, so no cross-repo access is involved, exactly as growth-extract reads `git log` and
22	  stages its lessons. Opening the lesson PR and arming its auto-merge, posting the summary, and the
23	  tracking-issue log go through the session's GitHub MCP tools (`mcp__github__*`) — none of those is a
24	  plain-git operation.
25	- **The repo's local packs.** Everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the canon home repo's own is
26	  `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/`; the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` is accepted during the rename
27	  window); never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
28	
29	## The run
30	
31	1. **Fetch the queue.** `git fetch origin conversation-logs`; list its files
32	   (`git ls-tree --name-only origin/conversation-logs`). No branch, or no `*.jsonl` → stop; a quiet repo is
33	   the common, valid outcome.
34	2. **Read retention.** From this repo's `.claudinite-checks.json`, the grow_with_claudinite entry's
35	   `config.retention_days`. Unset → the prune in step 5 is skipped entirely (capture-only adoption). (The
36	   precondition already declined to dispatch a quiet repo whose retention is unset, so on a quiet dispatch you
37	   will have retention set.)
38	3. **Fresh pass.** For each log captured in the recent window (its filename carries the capture stamp; corpus
39	   dedup makes an overlapping re-read harmless, so err toward re-reading the last several days): read it
40	   (`git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`) and run the extracting-lessons method over it — including the
41	   wall-time/efficiency analysis, measured from the log's own timestamps, never hand-waved.
42	4. **Route, land, and post.** Fold each keeper into the repo's **own local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`)
43	   at the local promotion ladder's strongest mechanism, exactly as
44	   [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) prescribes — landing the whole run through **one
45	   auto-merging PR** (title `Claudinite growth: conversation extract`, its commit referencing the worked issue
46	   so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes), armed for auto-merge the same way
47	   [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) delivers: GitHub squash-merges it once the repo's checks pass,
48	   with no human review. For each rule that actually landed, post **one short comment** via
49	   `add_issue_comment` on the issue named in the log's filename (`--issue-<n>--`): one provenance line (the
50	   rule added, the capture date, the session id), then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of
51	   conversation that caused the rule — what was asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule
52	   follows from it. Summarize, never transcribe: the dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue, so no
53	   pasted turns beyond a short quoted phrase, and never the log. A log that yields nothing gets **no**
54	   comment — extraction is the only path to permanence. Finding nothing at all is fine and common.
55	5. **Retention prune.** When `retention_days` is set: for each log whose filename stamp is older than
56	   `retention_days` days, give it a **final hindsight pass** — one last read against the now-current corpus
57	   (steps 3–4 apply to anything it still yields) — then `git rm` it on the `conversation-logs` branch and push
58	   (commit message ending `[skip ci]`). The branch is never merged and its history is never rewritten — plain
59	   add/remove commits only. This push to the non-default logs branch is outside the outcome taxonomy (DESIGN §1).
60	
61	## Tracking: log each run under the task's own issue
62	
63	The standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Conversation Extract`** in this repo —
64	found by that exact title, never a number; created **closed** if missing; its state never changed afterward.
65	When a run lands a lesson, posts a summary, or prunes logs, log it as one dated comment (via
66	`add_issue_comment`) naming what changed; a run that changed nothing logs nothing.
67	
68	## Run on a capable model
69	
70	Whether a lesson clears the bar — and whether the hindsight pass should overturn a fresh-pass call — is the
71	judgment this task exists for, and its PR auto-merges without a human review gate. This task declares
72	`model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.
73	
74	## What this task must never do
75	
76	- **Never merge `conversation-logs`** anywhere, and never rewrite its history — plain add and remove commits
77	  only.
78	- **Never paste the conversation onto an issue** — not raw JSONL, not a rendered transcript, not the turns
79	  themselves. Each landed rule gets one ≤200-word summary of the exchange behind it, and nothing more.
80	- **Never delete a log younger than retention, and never delete anything while `retention_days` is unset** —
81	  deletion is the ack that both passes happened.
82	- **Never touch the shared canon** — writes go to the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/` (via an
83	  auto-merging PR), its issues, and its logs branch; lifting portable lessons is the central promote task's job.

SKILL.md
---LEGACY---

1	# Extracting lessons from a working session
2	
3	> **Scope: a single agent ↔ user conversation.** This doc is the **method** for mining one
4	> working session's *dialogue and the actions taken in it* for improvements. It is **not** the
5	> growth extract ([extract.md](extract.md)) that mines **issues, PRs, and commits** over repo
6	> history — that routine never sees a conversation. Its two callers: the
7	> [conversation-extract daily task](conversation-extract.md), which applies it to **captured**
8	> conversation logs — where the friction signals below (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a
9	> wait you sat through) survive with their timestamps — and an owner's occasional plain-words
10	> ask for a retrospective over the live session.
11	
12	Portable guidance for mining an agent ↔ user session — a Claude Code web session, a CLI run, a
13	captured conversation log — for durable improvements: read the conversation and convert its
14	friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less dependent on human
15	feedback.
16	
17	Run the reflection on a **capable model.** Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears
18	the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong
19	"lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
20	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model
21	to the judgment it must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the
22	separate efficiency analysis — also live there; this doc is the how-to.
23	
24	## The goal
25	
26	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less
27	rework, less waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but
28	as "where did this cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost
29	next time." If a pass can't name a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's
30	fine (see [No new lessons](#no-new-lessons-is-a-valid--and-common--result)).
31	
32	## When it runs
33	
34	Routinely, in the [conversation-extract daily task](conversation-extract.md) over each captured
35	log (a fresh pass within a day of capture, a final hindsight pass before retention deletes the
36	log) — the standard path. If an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective over the live
37	session, apply the same method and deliver the capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**,
38	never one that self-merges (the nightly auto-merges its own PR per its own doc; a live retrospective
39	wants human eyes). **Never
40	reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner
41	decides when a session is done enough to mine.
42	
43	## What to look for — the friction signals
44	
45	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop
46	cost more than necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
47	
48	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
49	
50	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I
51	meant…"); the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same
52	request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
53	
54	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every
55	question the user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate
56	**convention or glossary entry**; a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first
57	checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc the agent reads cold and gets right the first
58	time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds correctly **without the round-trip**.
59	
60	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
61	
62	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran
63	a command that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light
64	one fit; reinvented something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written
65	to "verify"; missed an existing convention and had it corrected in review.
66	
67	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing
68	helper/convention so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read.** Place
69	it by where the trap is hit, not in a central bucket: a gotcha from **misusing a specific API,
70	class, or library goes as a comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where
71	the next editor of that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list.
72	Co-locate it in a file's own header comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only
73	hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a central gotchas doc for what no single usage site
74	owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant file (a mistake of omission), or a
75	cross-cutting invariant. The test: next time the agent takes the good path first, not after a
76	detour.
77	
78	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
79	
80	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been
81	parallel; a padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its
82	result was already in hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already
83	green.
84	
85	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers and separate the
86	kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting** (sleeps,
87	polling, a finished process not yet killed). A captured log carries per-entry timestamps and
88	per-message token usage, so the numbers are computable, not estimated. A fix is only credible
89	against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
90	was already optimal.
91	
92	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
93	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the
94	subject of the standing **efficiency analysis** in
95	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold a wall-time
96	finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
97	loss of quality.
98	
99	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
100	
101	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks
102	*repeatedly* are a checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how
103	many processes ran — could it be fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its
104	work was done?", stop waiting to be asked — fold those exact questions into a **standing
105	self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the relevant work, and close with a
106	terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each recurring question
107	converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
108	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively,
109	with numbers.
110	
111	## From signal to lesson — the bar
112	
113	A friction signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and
114	generalizable beyond this one session.** Before adding anything:
115	
116	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded
117	  differently, even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
118	- **Route to the local pack that owns it, and prefer the strongest mechanism** — the **local
119	  promotion ladder**, at the project's own level. A project's capture surface is its **local
120	  packs** (`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/`): pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs
121	  to, then a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (its failure message
122	  *is* the lesson; ship it with a red-first fixture), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a
123	  **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's
124	  `RULES.md`. Write more checks and less prose — a check relieves every session's context
125	  completely where prose only relocates it. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a
126	  comment at that site (above), not into any pack. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson
127	  warrants segregation, a new local pack is a self-contained directory drop.
128	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared,
129	  cross-project canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote
130	  stage lifts it there centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever
131	  travels.
132	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or
133	  something already implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
134	
135	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
136	
137	Most sessions yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write nothing
138	rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes
139	the canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a
140	genuinely new, reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
141

===== edfringe/RULES.md =====
# EdFringeNow — project working rules

Lessons captured while working in this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite
canon. Terse and concrete; read the matching one before working in that area.

## Verifying UI changes visually (the `index.html` page and everything under `plan/`)

Visual verification of the pages **is** available in this sandbox. Don't skip it
or downgrade to "verified by logic review only" claiming no browser exists — a
browser is here, and a UI change isn't done until it has been looked at.

- Serve the repo and drive it with the preinstalled Chromium (or Playwright):
  `python3 -m http.server 8000`, then screenshot / click through
  `http://localhost:8000`. The app fetches `data/shows.json`, so it must be
  served over HTTP rather than opened as a file — and `localhost` bypasses the
  agent proxy, so the browser reaches the page even though external hosts need
  the proxy.
- To build a `/plan` favourites list for the render, a plain slug-per-line text
  file is accepted by the parser — pick shows spanning the statuses (and some
  same-day doubles) you want to eyeball.
- **Never chain `pkill -f "http.server …"` with the rest of a command.** `-f`
  matches full command lines, so the pattern matches the very shell running the
  `pkill`: the shell kills itself (exit 144) and everything after the `;` or
  `&&` — the commit, the verify run, the curl — silently never happens. Every
  such call in this repo's captured sessions died this way, once misdiagnosed as
  a heredoc bug. Bracket a character so the pattern can't match its own command
  line (`pkill -f "[h]ttp.server 8099"`), or just leave the server up and serve
  the next run on a fresh port.
- **Known-noisy console output from the served page.** A page driven off
  `python3 -m http.server` reliably logs a `favicon.ico` 404 (the repo ships
  none) and often `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` as the browser tears down. Neither
  is an application error — filter both out of a smoke script's error assertion
  so that a red run means something, rather than sending you chasing a phantom
  404 through extra browser runs.
- To match edfringe.com's live styling (e.g. the ticket-availability colours on
  the `/plan` grid), fetch the official site's CSS with `curl` through the agent
  proxy and read the palette out of it. `WebFetch` returns rendered text without
  the CSS, and headless Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy to reach an external
  host — `curl` is the one path that works for off-box assets.

## The site is two independent front-ends — cross-page behaviour lives twice

The Now page (`index.html` + `js/app.js`) and the planner (`plan/` + `plan/plan.js`)
share no code: no modules, no globals, and `plan/lib/` is the planner's own engine,
not a common library. So anything that must behave the same on both pages exists as
**two copies**, and changing one is only half the change — the UK-bounding-box
location guard and the debug menu it gates, the header `debug v<version>` pill, and
the Now/Plan nav each live in both files today. Grep the other file for the twin
before calling a cross-page change done; it will not fail a test or a parse check.
===== edfringe-data/RULES.md =====
# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)

The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
judgment those two don't carry.

## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it

`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and
`edfringe.com` returns 403 to `WebFetch`. So: no session — this one included —
can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
runs on a GitHub-hosted runner: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets`
scheduled tasks, or the throwaway probe procedure in the `probe-edfringe-api`
skill. Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
returns — either run it on a runner, or say plainly that it is unverified.

`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
offline (it is a step in `scripts/verify.sh`); it exercises
raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a normalizer change is
verifiable here even though a fetch change is not.

## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean

"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
carried through for display only.

## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it

`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.

## Changing the wire format is a four-file change

The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`, `p[].t`).
That encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:

- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
  `minify_master`)
- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`

Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.

8:Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the engineering-practices skill](../engineering-practices/SKILL.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)
25:- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.

7:An interactive comment from the owner carries one of three build-relevant intents — or none of them — and the classification decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part) — the assessment itself stays judgment.
8-
9-1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched — the artifact changes as much as the correction demands; what doesn't appear is a new requirement or rule.
10-2. **A feature** — a feature run: agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
11-3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Once the intent is understood, author the assurance first: the check the future world must satisfy. Execute it and watch it fail — the failure is the evidence it detects exactly what the owner was worried about — and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the same step is demonstrating the gap: show the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
12-
13-The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it. A fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for — and an unrouted comment tends to become a one-off patch where a requirement or a rule should have accumulated.
14-
15-Confirm a behavior isn't already provided before building a mechanism for it — verify the gap against a real run first; the cheapest fix is often that it already works.

70:## A push or PR made with the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not start another workflow
72:GitHub suppresses workflow runs triggered by the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to prevent recursion, so a workflow's own `git push` or `gh pr create` won't fire another workflow (e.g. a `test` or cache-refresh workflow). The one exception is `workflow_dispatch` / `repository_dispatch` — which is why an automation pipeline that needs the downstream checks to run must dispatch them explicitly. A run dispatched against a branch executes on its head commit, so its checks still attach to the PR. The same suppression covers a Claude session's own app-scoped pushes: creating a PR through the API does fire its `pull_request` run, but a follow-up push to that PR gets **no** `synchronize` run — so don't wait for checks that will never start on the new head; gate by running the CI commands locally, and rely on the post-merge run (merging through the merge API does fire the `push` workflow on the default branch).
76:A `workflow_dispatch` or scheduled workflow runs from the copy on the **default branch**, and a `pull_request` run uses the workflow files from the PR's **base** branch — so a workflow you only added on a feature branch isn't dispatchable, and a build/CI change doesn't apply, until it's merged. Merge workflow and build-script changes *before* the release or run that depends on them, or that run executes the *old* definition (shipping a stale build, or silently skipping a check you thought you'd added). This is distinct from the `GITHUB_TOKEN` recursion rule above: even a human-triggered run reads the definition from the default/base branch, not your feature branch.
118:A `push` or `workflow_dispatch` run isn't attached to a PR, so the PR-scoped check-run query above doesn't apply to it. Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.

1	# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose
2	
3	Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted.
4	
5	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
6	
7	The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).
8	
9	## The method lives in the skill
10	
11	The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.
12	
13	## What a run does
14	
15	1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert) and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
16	2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Trim the now-redundant prose to rationale.
17	3. **Open a PR** — one PR for the run's conversions on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. Keep the repo's offline test suite green before opening.
18	4. **Log to the tracker** — the standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".
19

# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose

Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted.

You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.

The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).

## The method lives in the skill

The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.

## What a run does

1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert) and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Trim the now-redundant prose to rationale.
3. **Open a PR** — one PR for the run's conversions on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. Keep the repo's offline test suite green before opening.
4. **Log to the tracker** — the standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".

## What this task must never do

- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
- **Never touch a pack path outside the Context**, and **never edit a mounted canon pack** under `.claudinite/shared/` — a consumer improves only its own local packs.
- **Run on `opus`** — judging convertibility and authoring checks + fixtures is heavy judgment; this task declares `agent_model: opus`.

1	---
2	name: prose-to-checks
3	description: Mine a repo's existing pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, or when the growth prose-to-checks sweep runs.
4	---
5	
6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs. The growth *extract* stage converts each **new**
9	lesson down the promotion ladder; this pass sweeps the **existing** prose backlog for rules that
10	are always-testable but still live only as prose — and converts them, so the packs keep shedding
11	context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is first learned. It runs as
12	grow_with_claudinite's daily `prose-to-checks-sweep` task, and on demand.
13	
14	## Scope — the pack paths you were given
15	
16	Work only the **pack paths configured for this repo** (the task passes them in its Context): a
17	consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by default — projects don't
18	improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core `packs/`. Read the
19	prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them). Never edit a
20	read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
21	
22	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
23	
24	For each rule, ask the one question from
25	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
26	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
27	
28	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
29	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
30	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
31	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
32	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
33	
34	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
35	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
36	
37	## How to convert one
38	
39	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
40	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
41	
42	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
43	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
44	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
45	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
46	   doesn't ship.
47	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
48	   directional by kind.
49	4. **Trim the prose** to rationale — the check owns enforcement now; leaving both pays twice and
50	   springs the drift trap.
51	
52	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
53	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
54	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
55	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
56	check to the same fixture bar.
57	
58	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
59	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.
60	
61	## Bounds
62	
63	- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
64	  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
65	- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — trimming prose is only for a rule a *landed* check
66	  now enforces.
67	- Run the suite and the sweep green before opening the PR; open it for the owner's approval,
68	  never a direct push to `main`.

1	# EdFringeNow — project working rules
2	
3	Lessons captured while working in this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite
4	canon. Terse and concrete; read the matching one before working in that area.
5	
6	## Verifying UI changes visually (the `index.html` page and everything under `plan/`)
7	
8	Visual verification of the pages **is** available in this sandbox. Don't skip it
9	or downgrade to "verified by logic review only" claiming no browser exists — a
10	browser is here, and a UI change isn't done until it has been looked at.
11	
12	- Serve the repo and drive it with the preinstalled Chromium (or Playwright):
13	  `python3 -m http.server 8000`, then screenshot / click through
14	  `http://localhost:8000`. The app fetches `data/shows.json`, so it must be
15	  served over HTTP rather than opened as a file — and `localhost` bypasses the
16	  agent proxy, so the browser reaches the page even though external hosts need
17	  the proxy.
18	- To build a `/plan` favourites list for the render, a plain slug-per-line text
19	  file is accepted by the parser — pick shows spanning the statuses (and some
20	  same-day doubles) you want to eyeball.
21	- **Never chain `pkill -f "http.server …"` with the rest of a command.** `-f`
22	  matches full command lines, so the pattern matches the very shell running the
23	  `pkill`: the shell kills itself (exit 144) and everything after the `;` or
24	  `&&` — the commit, the verify run, the curl — silently never happens. Every
25	  such call in this repo's captured sessions died this way, once misdiagnosed as
26	  a heredoc bug. Bracket a character so the pattern can't match its own command
27	  line (`pkill -f "[h]ttp.server 8099"`), or just leave the server up and serve
28	  the next run on a fresh port.
29	- **Known-noisy console output from the served page.** A page driven off
30	  `python3 -m http.server` reliably logs a `favicon.ico` 404 (the repo ships
31	  none) and often `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` as the browser tears down. Neither
32	  is an application error — filter both out of a smoke script's error assertion
33	  so that a red run means something, rather than sending you chasing a phantom
34	  404 through extra browser runs.
35	- To match edfringe.com's live styling (e.g. the ticket-availability colours on
36	  the `/plan` grid), fetch the official site's CSS with `curl` through the agent
37	  proxy and read the palette out of it. `WebFetch` returns rendered text without
38	  the CSS, and headless Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy to reach an external
39	  host — `curl` is the one path that works for off-box assets.
40	
41	## The site is two independent front-ends — cross-page behaviour lives twice
42	
43	The Now page (`index.html` + `js/app.js`) and the planner (`plan/` + `plan/plan.js`)
44	share no code: no modules, no globals, and `plan/lib/` is the planner's own engine,
45	not a common library. So anything that must behave the same on both pages exists as
46	**two copies**, and changing one is only half the change — the UK-bounding-box
47	location guard and the debug menu it gates, the header `debug v<version>` pill, and
48	the Now/Plan nav each live in both files today. Grep the other file for the twin
49	before calling a cross-page change done; it will not fail a test or a parse check.
50

1	# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)
2	
3	The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
4	committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
5	under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
6	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
7	[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
8	judgment those two don't carry.
9	
10	## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it
11	
12	`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and
13	`edfringe.com` returns 403 to `WebFetch`. So: no session — this one included —
14	can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
15	runs on a GitHub-hosted runner: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
16	(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets`
17	scheduled tasks, or the throwaway probe procedure in the `probe-edfringe-api`
18	skill. Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
19	returns — either run it on a runner, or say plainly that it is unverified.
20	
21	`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
22	offline (it is a step in `scripts/verify.sh`); it exercises
23	raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a normalizer change is
24	verifiable here even though a fetch change is not.
25	
26	## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean
27	
28	"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
29	`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
30	sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
31	`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
32	(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
33	availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
34	carried through for display only.
35	
36	## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it
37	
38	`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
39	`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
40	fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
41	`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
42	full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
43	`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.
44	
45	## Changing the wire format is a four-file change
46	
47	The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
48	**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`, `p[].t`).
49	That encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:
50	
51	- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
52	  `minify_master`)
53	- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
54	- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
55	  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
56	  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`
57	
58	Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
59	indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
60	catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
61	decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.
62

{
  "name": "edfringenow",
  "version": "1.0727.13",
  "private": true,
  "description": "EdFringeNow — client-side Edinburgh Fringe discovery + planner. No runtime dependencies; a build/serve-free static site.",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "node --test plan/lib/__tests__/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/*/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/edfringe/tasks/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/edfringe/tasks/*/*.test.mjs",
    "verify": "bash scripts/verify.sh",
    "setup-hooks": "bash scripts/setup-hooks.sh"
  }
}
=== verify.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# The repo's single verification gate: unit tests, JavaScript parse-checks, and
# Python byte-compilation. Both the pre-commit hook (.githooks/pre-commit) and
# CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) run *this* script, so "green locally" and
# "green on GitHub" mean exactly the same thing.
#
# Fast (well under a second) and dependency-free — everything uses the node /
# python already needed to work on the project.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"

step() { printf '\n\033[1m▶ %s\033[0m\n' "$1"; }

step "Unit tests — node --test"
# The planner's own tests, plus the local packs' — one glob for each pack's own
# pack.test.mjs (its checks' red-first fixtures), one for the shared task
# declaration test, one for the per-task tests beside each task. Those tests import
# every pack manifest and task declaration, so they are also what parse-checks that
# tree (the syntax sweep below deliberately stays off the .claudinite mount).
# Keep in step with the "test" script in package.json.
node --test plan/lib/__tests__/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/*/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/edfringe/tasks/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/edfringe/tasks/*/*.test.mjs

step "JavaScript syntax — node --check"
# Only our own tracked source: the js/ app and the plan/ planner. Never the
# vendored .claudinite mount (not our code) or the plan/design/ mock (HTML).
js_files=$(git ls-files 'js' 'plan' | { grep -E '\.m?js$' || true; } | { grep -v '^plan/design/' || true; })
js_count=0
for f in $js_files; do
  node --check "$f"
  js_count=$((js_count + 1))
done
echo "checked ${js_count} JavaScript file(s)"

step "Python syntax — py_compile"
py_files=$(git ls-files 'scraper/*.py')
if [ -z "$py_files" ]; then
  echo "no Python sources found — skipping"
elif command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  # shellcheck disable=SC2086
  python3 -m py_compile $py_files
  echo "checked $(printf '%s\n' $py_files | wc -l | tr -d ' ') Python file(s)"
else
  echo "python3 not installed — skipping (CI always has it)" >&2
fi

step "Normalizer self-test — normalize.py --selftest"
# Exercises the raw→master→day-file→shows.min.json transforms on a fixture (no
# network / no raw data), so the packer and the day-file builder are covered here
# and the round-trip decoder is covered by plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs.
if command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest
else
  echo "python3 not installed — skipping (CI always has it)" >&2
fi

printf '\n\033[32m✓ all checks passed\033[0m\n'

- **Launch Playwright with no `executablePath`, and import from `index.mjs`.**
  `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers` is already exported in this
  sandbox, so `chromium.launch()` finds its browser on its own. Every captured
  session instead hand-wrote a path and paid for it: `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium`
  is a *directory*, and the real binary sits under a version-pinned
  `chromium-<build>/chrome-linux/chrome` that moves with the image. Import the
  global build by its ESM entry —
  `import { chromium } from '/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'`
  (the sibling `index.js` is CJS, so a *named* import from it yields
  `undefined`) — or `$(npm root -g)/playwright/index.mjs` if the prefix moved.
  Path discovery and its sed-fix-up round-trips cost ~220s across five captured
  sessions, every one of them re-deriving the same two facts.
- **Keep one browser driver script per session and re-point it.** Authoring a
  fresh throwaway Playwright script per screenshot cost 29 heredoc writes and

{"number":90,"title":"Planner: editable favourites, unified debug pill, draggable dates, trip blocks","body":"## What & why

A batch of planner UX changes so the grid is the editable source of truth, the debug affordances are tidier, and the schedule accounts for arrival/departure.

### Debug + grid editing
- **DEBUG now adds, not replaces.** "Add 10 random shows" *appends* to the current set (de-duped) instead of wiping it.
- **Remove a row from the grid.** Each row has an `×`; removing a show writes straight back to the stored favourites (localStorage). Before the first screenshot could be taken, the agent had to work out how to launch a browser at all: it first imported Playwright with a named `import { chromium } from '…/index.js'`, which silently yields `undefined` (that entry is CommonJS), then pointed `executablePath` at `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium` — a directory, not a binary — and had to `find` the version-pinned `chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome` and `sed` the script twice before it ran. 123s of pure discovery, and the same two mistakes recur in four other captured sessions (~220s total). `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` is already exported in this sandbox, so no `executablePath` was ever needed.

The session then authored 16 separate throwaway driver scripts, one per shot, at 15–20s each — 4.5 minutes of wall clock that one argv-driven, re-run driver would have avoided.

The UK-mainland bounding box is the one twin on that list with a static projection: `const UK_BOUNDS = { minLat: 49.8, maxLat: 59.0, minLng: -8.2, maxLng: 1.9 }` appears in `js/app.js:36` (gating the Now page's location guard) and `plan/plan.js:1066` (gating the planner's debug menu), with nothing tying them together.

Reordered keys, rewrapped lines, a different comment, `59.0` vs `59` — none of it is drift. A mention of the name in a comment elsewhere is not mistaken for a copy.
